cf182b4827eff45a1babde07203564e2.text: Margaret (Marg) Bublitz, 80, said receiving the Lifetime Achievement Award came as a surprise. Holding her Lifetime Achievement Award, Margaret (Marg) Bublitz reflects on more than five decades of volunteering in Williams Lake. Margaret (Marg) Bublitz celebrated her 80th birthday and received the Lifetime Achievement Award at the Williams Lake and District Chamber of Commerce's Business Excellence Awards, surrounded by family. She wrote in the Facebook post, "Just to have so much family here to support me on Saturday night was amazing. My heart is so full." The Lifetime Achievement Award, sponsored by The GOAT & Cariboo Country Radio. For longtime Williams Lake volunteerMargaret (Marg) Bublitz, her husband has some advice for her whenever she decides to head to a meeting: learn to sit on your hands. So, when someone needs a treasurer, a letter written or help keeping a community event alive, Bublitz has a familiar response. Bublitz’s family had planned to celebrate her 80th birthday. Instead, they gathered to watch her receive a Lifetime Achievement Award recognizing decades of volunteering in Williams Lake. The Life Achievement Award was presented during the annual Williams Lake & District Chamber of Commerce Business Excellence Awards on a Saturday evening Oct. 24. “If there’s something that needs doing, I’m there right?”, said Bublitz. For Bublitz, volunteering has been a way to spend time with others while helping get things done. She raised two children in Williams Lake, bringing them along while she volunteered at the Stampede and Williams Lake Harvest fair. Her commitments grew out of interest she wanted to to make make room for alongside work and family. Before learning she had won, Bublitz already felt honoured to be nominated. “I was very shocked that I was nominated. And that was enough for me,” she said. “I don’t think of myself as old,” she added while expressing how surprised she was in the terms suggested by a Lifetime Achievement Award. The Saturday

Cariboo Chilcotin Coast Tourism Association Chair Angela Bissat presents an award to George Vanderwolf during the CCCT's AGM. The Cariboo Chilcotin Coast Tourism Association elected a new board during its annual Tourism Summit and AGM last week. Held in Lillooet, the AGM drew tourism operators from across the region. During the summit, attendees elected a new board, honoured 2026’s award winners and listened to guest speakers. “The Tourism Summit is about connections across the Cariboo Chilcotin Coast and the incredible variety of operators and officials who work so hard to protect and enhance the tourism sector,” Amy Thacker, CEO of Cariboo Chilcotin Coast Tourism CCCT, said. “There is so much to celebrate and so much to share and the region is a special place for the travelling public thanks to all the wonderful communities and people.” Thacker added that the summit was its usual blend of good times at the gala, insight from speakers and association business. She highlighted that the CCCT received a clean audit this year from Doane Grant Thornton, who found that 80 cents of every dollar goes into CCCT programs. In 2027, Thacker said the CCCT’s priority will be renewing its contract with Destination BC. During the 2026 CCCT Awards Gala held on Oct. 20, Thacker said several awards were given out to organizations and individuals. Each recipient received a jade trophy carved by Lillooet artisan George Vanderwolf. They included the Innovation in Tourism Award, which went to the Jakira Foundation for the accessible wilderness adventures they run on Quesnel Lake. The Best Tourism Marketing Initiative Award, meanwhile, went to Barkerville Historic Town & Park for its “Barkerville: The Series,” a YouTube show dramatizing life at the site. On May 26, 2026 the founder of the Cow Moose Moose Sign Project received an award commemorating him being a finalist of the inaugural Dr. Valerius Geist Conservation Legacy Award. It was launched by Hunters for BC to recognize those who continue the legacy of the renowned scientist who was also a hunter, storyteller, naturalist and mentor by making meaningful contributions to wildlife and habitat conservation across North America. Simmons was nominated by Hunters for BC vice president Dave Ryder who retired from the B.C.-based, hunter-led non-profit conservation organization earlier this month. As one of seven distinguished finalists from across Canada and the U.S. Simmons was presented with a hand-engraved glass award he said he received on his 72nd birthday by Purolator. “It took about 30 pictures,” Dan remarked of finally getting just the right one of him smiling with his wife Vivian as they held the award with Horsefly Lake in the background. 58a4bb201e525246ae19a15e4b5640f3.text: Vancouver Canucks centre Elias Pettersson fires a shot during NHL action Thursday, Oct 29, 2026 against the San Jose Sharks at the SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. Will Smith scored a pair of goals, leading the San Jose Sharks to a come-from-behind 3-2 win over the visiting Vancouver Canucks in NHL action Thursday at the SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. Mason Marchment also scored for the Sharks (7-6-1), who trailed 2-0 midway through the third period. Yaroslav Askarov made 23 saves to earn the win in goal. Drew O’Connor and Liam Öhgren scored for the Canucks (3-11-1), who ended a 10-game losing skid Tuesday in Anaheim. Leevi Merilainen stopped 21 of 24 shots and took the loss for Vancouver. O’Connor scored the lone goal of the first period, driving to the net and knocking home a rebound off a shot from centre Elias Pettersson at 13:21. O’Connor now has two goals on the season and Pettersson is on a six-game point-scoring streak. Öhgren upped the lead to 2-0 with just 1:04 left in the second period, ripping a shot past Askarov from about 20 feet out near the right faceoff circle for his fourth of the year. Smith pulled San Jose within one eight minutes into the second on the power play, moving in from the point and beating Merilainen from the top of the right circle with his fifth of the season. With 9:21 left in the period, Smith struck again, taking a nifty pass from Macklin Celebrini and beating Merilainen for his second of the game. Just 11 seconds after that, the Sharks controlled the faceoff and Marchment moved down the left side and fired a shot through Merilainen to give San Jose a 3-2 lead. On a late power play in the third, the Canucks pulled Merilainen to create a 6-on-4 situation but were unable to convert and the Sharks hung on for the win. c9397c67db640a21667ac8866300603f.text: Community Foundation North Okanagan presents $10,000 to Okanagan Indian Band Chief and Council for food security work after the Bradley Creek wildfire, September 8, 2026. Support continues to make its way to people affected by the Bradley Creek wildfire near Vernon. Community Foundation North Okanagan (CFNO) has granted $55,000 from the Wildfire Response 2026 Fund to 13 local organizations supporting people displaced by the blaze that rapidly spread on Aug. 1. The grants are funding food security, mental health support help for families who were evacuated or lost property, animal rescue, and services for newcomers and Indigenous residents. The fund was established on Aug. 5 as a trusted local place to give after the Bradley Creek wildfire forced evacuations across the North Okanagan. Since then, 471 donors have contributed $348,716. The fund is still open and more granting is planned, at cfno.org/wildfire-response-2026. This first round of grants went to organizations already on the ground, in direct contact with people who had been evacuated or had lost homes. “Granting locally means support arrives through people who already know their neighbours and can direct it where it will do the most good,” the CFNO said. **Okanagan Indian Band:** $23,000 across three grants. An early $3,000 went out on Aug. 7 for immediate needs. In September, CFNO presented $10,000 to Chief and Council for food security work, helping replace food lost during evacuations and restock fridges, freezers and pantries, and a further $10,000 to the What Happens Upstream youth conference, supporting young people affected by the fire. Donors who wished to support OKIB programs directly were also able to give through the OKIB Fund. **School District 22:** $10,000. Supporting 21 families across five schools who were displaced by the fire. The district has been helping families purchase clothing, household necessities and groceries, and has made breakfasts, lunches, snacks and take-home meals

08bed510576b88ddde73cf130e47e214.text: Dorothy Alexander (second from left) with some of the students at My School (now the Alternative Learning Program) in 1988. A woman who spent nearly a lifetime dedicated to caring for and supporting those with disabilities is being fondly remembered. Isabella Dorothy Alexander died Oct. 1, 2026 at the age of 87. Better known as Dorothy, her contributions to the Vernon area touched countless lives and continue to be felt through the community. “Dorothy Alexander was not only a remarkable advocate for persons with disabilities in our community, but also a true pioneer whose vision and dedication helped shape the services and opportunities available today,” said Ryan Cucheron, chief executive officer of Venture Living – formerly Venture Training, which Alexander was on the founding board of. While born in Manitoba, Alexander grew up in Spallumcheen’s Hullcar area and went to Armstrong Elementary School. After high school she furthered her education and began a lifelong commitment to helping others. “Dorothy became a passionate advocate for people with disabilities, working to ensure they had opportunities to learn, participate, and live with dignity,” her obituary reads. Playing an important role in the early development of services for people with disabilities in Vernon, in 1958 Alexander started at My School providing education and activities for 10 children with disabilities (and that number continued to grow). Under her leadership, the program flourished, eventually expanding and relocating to what is now Venture Living’s main location on Alexis Park Drive, according to Cucheron. “During the 1960s and 1970s, Dorothy used approaches that were truly groundbreaking for their time,” he said. “While community inclusion may seem like a natural expectation today, her efforts to bring individuals with disabilities into the community challenged the prevailing attitudes of institutionalization. She believed strongly that individuals with disabilities deserved opportunities

A judge might decide whether Surrey will have a school trustee byelection at a cost of close to $840,000. The situation involves Garry Thind, re-elected trustee on Oct. 17 and then elected Conservative MLA in Surrey-Guildford a week later, Oct. 24. Once sworn in as MLA in coming weeks, Thind will be disqualified from being a school trustee, Surrey Schools confirms. Moving forward, if a court application is made under the Local Government Act, a judge can order that the trustee position is vacant, resulting in a byelection, or order that the candidate who received the next-highest number of votes — incumbent Gary Tymoschuk, in this case — be declared elected in place of the disqualified candidate, says a school district statement sent Thursday, Oct. 29. Under the legislation, the Chief Election Officer, a candidate in the election, or any four electors may apply to the court for a determination, the *Now-Leader* is told. “Any application must be filed within 30 days of the certification of the election results, which is November 20,” Surrey Schools says in an email. “As a result, the District cannot comment on what Garry Thind’s election as an MLA means for filling the final Board seat or the possibility of any byelection. That will depend on whether a court application is made and, if so, how the court rules.” The district statement adds: “Initial cost estimates provided to Surrey Schools by the City of Surrey place the cost of a byelection at approximately $840,000. Fire at Creative Studies building on the UBCO campus, Oct. 29. Fire crews on scene of blaze at the Creative Studies building on UBCO campus. Fire crews on scene of blaze at the Creative Studies building on UBCO campus. A fire that broke out at the Creative and Critical Studies building at UBC Okanagan has been contained, according to the Kelowna Fire Department (KFD). The blaze, which started at around 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 29, was extinguished due to the efforts of the KFD, who deployed 30 firefighters, five engines and two ladder trucks to the scene. Deputy Fire Chief Larry Watkinson told reporters at the scene that the preliminary investigations suggest the fire was started due to construction work on the roof of the building. “Behind the cladding is an insulated foam packaging, and it caught fire. It ran up the inside of the cladding which got into the structure, and that’s how the fire started,” Watkinson said. He added that no one was found inside the building as fire crews arrived, and no students or firefighters were injured. The deputy fire chief said the fire was contained and there was “very limited” impact to any of the classrooms in the connecting building. Still, the original structure suffered some smoke and water damage. A blaze in the roof of the Creative and Critical Studies building, has caused an evacuation as fire crews continue to douse the smoke and flame. All classes and exams in the building are cancelled until further notice. Additional student supports are available at students.ok.ubc.ca/support/support-for-unanticipated-circumstances. A large fire is burning inside the Creative Studies building on the University of British Columbia Okanagan campus. Huge plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the building just after 12 p.m. According to those on campus, flames can also be seen coming from the building.

c89da9a40bdfc0ff9f01bb624c8cdf92.text: Kendal and Geoff Bourdon with Woodland Jewellers hope to raise $12,000 this year through their annual raffle supporting the Cariboo Memorial Hospital Foundation. The 18-karat yellow gold valued at $9,900 features a teal sapphire accented with champagne diamonds. Geoff Bourdon likes pushing himself every year with designing and handcrafting a one-of-a-kind piece of jewellery raising funds for the Cariboo Memorial Hospital Foundation. Since 2009 the fourth generation owner of Woodland Jewellers has annually designed an exquisite raffle prize that has now raised $190,000 for the not-for-profit to purchase medical equipment for the Cariboo Memorial Hospital. This year’s prize is an 18-karat yellow gold ring featuring a teal sapphire accented with champagne diamonds. It is valued at $9,900. “If we sell out the tickets we’re going to break over the $200,000 mark for fundraisers,” said Woodland Jewellers manager and bookkeeper, Kendal Bourdon, who is also Geoff’s wife. About 30 hours of fabrication to make the ring was spent by Geoff who also mixed the 18-karat gold. He spent months, however, in advance on the design process. “I normally always start with the gemstone,” Geoff said, adding he believes his work should always complement the gemstone that is the centre of the piece. “If there’s a gemstone that I really want to work with then the design comes from the gemstone. Even this year the shape of the ring is a reflection of the cut of the gemstone, and the colours having the fancy natural round diamonds in the yellow gold brings out a lot of the green and the teal in the sapphire.” Each piece of jewellery he has presented in the annual raffle prize since 2009 is unique with Geoff pushing himself each year to do something he has either not technically or in style done before. 858097a3f7c147321b4972d61a6de839.text: The Quesnel River Rush played with the Quesnel Millionaires' jersey for Retro Night. **Thursday, Oct. 29 – Quesnel River Rush 3, Williams Lake Mustangs 11** The Quesnel River Rush watched a promising start unravel Thursday night as the Williams Lake Mustangs scored 10 goals over the final two periods in an 11-3 rout at the West Fraser Centre. On Thursday, Oct. 29, the River Rush opened the scoring exchanges with a strong start, keeping pace with Williams Lake through the first period. The Mustangs struck first when Kaelen Swanson scored at 2:31, but Quesnel responded just 26 seconds later as Luke Van Imschoot buried his ninth goal of the season on the power play at 2:57. The teams headed into the first intermission tied 1-1, with Quesnel showing early signs of being able to match the visiting Mustangs. Quesnel carried that momentum into the second period when Austin Root scored his first goal of the season at 3:24 to give the River Rush a 2-1 lead. However, Williams Lake quickly turned the game around. Kaden Charpentier tied the contest on the power play at 10:14 before Swanson scored twice in just over two minutes, including a power-play marker, to put the Mustangs ahead 4-2. Tristan Aidoo added another at 14:53, sending Williams Lake into the second intermission with a 5-2 advantage. The Mustangs continued to build their lead in the third period, with Logan Hauk scoring at 1:33. Quesnel’s Jimmy Proulx answered at 3:30 with his first goal of the season, briefly cutting into the deficit and making it 6-3. Williams Lake responded with five unanswered goals to close out the game. Braden Bolt scored at 4:30, followed by power-play goals from Chaz Lucas, Declan Pocock, Carter Krueger and Matthew Hufty as the Mustangs pulled away for the 11-3 victory. The Mustangs also controlled the shot count, outshooting Quesnel 54-31. Williams Lake recorded 28 shots in the third period alone, compared to just six for the River Rush. 13defaa82b9d2adb7072620f5a64dc69.text: "Hope they are safe," Donna Pryor wrote on Williams Lake Speak Up Facebook Thursday, Oct. 29 of her neighbours whose house was on fire. Williams Lake Fire Chief Evan Dean confirmed no injuries were reported. More than a dozen firefighters with the Williams Lake Fire Department were on the scene of a structure fire Thursday, Oct. 29. The department responded to reports of the blaze on Oak Place after receiving a call just before 9 p.m. reporting smoke and flame coming from the laundry room. Fire Chief and director of protective services Evan Dean noted the first responding officer reported considerable smoke as well as heat coming from the structure. “Firefighters were able to contain the fire and prevent further spread, however, smoke and fire damage were already extensive on arrival,” Dean added. “No injuries were reported and the fire is not considered suspicious.” A total of 18 firefighters responded with two command vehicles and two large apparatus were on scene for approximately two hours followed by a half hour of cleanup at the fire hall.

d5265745c8cb5b8b026c6b8d5c5407bd.text: Members of the Royal Canadian Air Force are able to training in aircraft maintenance engineering thanks to a new partnership with Okanagan College. Okanagan College’s Aircraft Maintenance Engineering is helping bolster Canada’s military and defence. Twenty-two members of the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) joined the college program in October. An agreement was signed by the two organizations to have RCAF members train at the Kelowna and Vernon airports. “This collaboration between the Royal Canadian Air Force and Okanagan College demonstrates how Canada’s government is protecting Canadians by forging new partnerships to strengthen our sovereignty and national security,” said Stephen Fuhr, Member of Parliament for Kelowna and Secretary of State for Defence Procurement. “This partnership is about diversifying training opportunities for new aircraft technicians at a time of growth for the RCAF,” said Brigadier-General Dan Coutts, Commander of 2 Canadian Air Division which is responsible for RCAF training. “This initiative is representative of the Defence Industrial Strategy, partnering with industry and academia to train technicians that will maintain the sophisticated aircraft of Canada’s Air Force today and into the future.” RCAF members will live in the college’s campus housing in Vernon during training. “We’re excited to be able to work in partnership with the Royal Canadian Air Force, helping to support their workforce demands and the efforts of the Canadian military, alongside our civilian cohorts of students,” said Caitlin Hartigan, Dean of Trades and Apprenticeship at Okanagan College. “There is significant demand for Aircraft Maintenance Engineers, and our program is focused on being agile and responsive in order to continue to produce skilled workers for the region and beyond.” The course is open to all students at Okanagan College with two aircraft maintenance programs, structures and mechanical.

f67b019fd01f8463699750f014a51983.text: A South Cariboo man has been arrested for several charges, including committing violence towards an intimate partner. On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the 100 Mile House RCMP and the Cariboo Crime Reduction Unit executed a search warrant at a residence located along the 5400-block of Canim Hendrix Lake Road. The warrant was executed in relation to allegations of threats. They were supported by the North District Emergency Response Team. Cpl. Jennifer Cooper said that during this operation, a man associated with the residence was located and arrested a short distance from the home. Cooper identified him as 36-year-old Dylan Ryder Gropp. Gropp has been charged with the following four offences: conspiracy to commit an indictable offence; uttering threats to burn, destroy or damage; criminal harassment and committing a violent offence against an intimate partner. None of these charges has been proven in a court of law. Cooper said that Gropp will remain in custody until his next court date.

6491b506fc505eb15007967a4cefdeda.text: The Canadian Wildfire Conference was held at the KF Centre for Excellence in Kelowna Oct. 28-29, 2026. A new precedent has been set for drought codes in British Columbia. At the Canadian Wildfire Conference, held at the KF Centre for Excellence in Kelowna on Oct. 28-29, B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) Provincial Aviation Specialist J.J. Lum provided a summary of the season. The French Bar weather station, the one nearest the Big Bar Complex, recorded drought levels above the 100th percentile of the 30-year average between May and mid-August. Weather stations nearest the Brunswick Complex and the Bald Range wildfire also recorded above the 100th percentile through August. “We were facing drought like we’ve never seen before,” Lum said, noting that the Bald Range wildfire sparked around the same time the drought code peaked in Penticton. Between Apr. 1 and Oct. 1, B.C. saw over 1,400 new fire starts and 10 wildfires of note, affecting more than 53,000 British Columbians across 53 communities and First Nations, and burning over 477,000 hectares. “The Cariboo Fire Centre, they were the big winner or the big loser depending on how you look at it, with 233 wildfires resulting in over 200,000 hectares burned,” Lum said. “To note, they are also the smallest fire centre.” The north saw a calmer season than normal, with the Northwest and Prince George centres combined seeing 218 wildfires burn 1,349 hectares. B.C.’s fire season was average for the number of fires, Lum said. “But really it’s not the number of wildfires you have, it’s where they start and how big they get.” Throughout the summer, BCWS deployed 1,863 personnel, engaged with 126 fire departments. The crews were also supported by fire personnel from across the globe, including multiple Canadian provinces and territories, Parks Canada, Canadian Forest Service, Mexico, Costa Rica, Australia and New Zealand. 5490cbc14230f5e4d8ed6ca2955867d8.text: Obama-backed doc film focused on Ghana produced by woman with B.C. roots | Williams Lake Tribune Obama-backed doc film focused on Ghana produced by woman with B.C. roots A scene from The Eyes of Ghana, a documentary film released in October 2026. Surrey-raised filmmaker Nana Adwoa Frimpong produced *The Eyes of Ghana*, an acclaimed documentary executive-produced by U.S. presidential couple Barack and Michelle Obama, Higher Ground founders. The 90-minute feature doc explores the life and work of 93-year-old Ghanaian filmmaker Chris Hesse, whose archive chronicles Ghana’s early years as a sovereign nation. Hesse served as personal cameraman to Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s first president. As his eyesight faded, Hesse rescued more than 1,000 films capturing the West Africa country’s fight for independence in the 1950s and 60s. The film, world-premiered a year ago at Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), is now in theatres across North America including Surrey’s Landmark Guildford on Sunday, Nov. 1. Frimpong, a director, writer and creative producer, says she’s thrilled to have the movie shown in her hometown. “My parents still live there (in Surrey) and they’re inviting everybody they know,” Frimpong said on the phone from New York City. “It’s exciting. I never dreamed that my home theatre would play a film that I produced. It’s very cool.” A Surrey resident until age 18, Frimpong now lives in Los Angeles and works for Breakwater Studios to “illuminate stories of women and people of colour,” the company website notes. Frimpong’s parents grew up in Ghana and later found a home in Canada with their children. “For me to be making a film like this, my first big film, and to have it call back to where my parents are from, where my sisters and I grew up knowing and believing was an extension of our home (in Canada), it’s a dream come true.” Frimpong’s passion for storytelling, the Breakwater website says, is marked by her past community organizing work around accessibility

Jazmyn Douillard with The Realm of Toys & The Nerd Room is extra happy for this year’s Downtown Trick r Treat in downtown Williams Lake. With Halloween falling on a Saturday, it was initially unclear if the annual festivities would be a go as many businesses, including professional services and government agencies, are closed on weekends. As it appeared there would be less than half the number of businesses participating from last year consideration was given to cancelling. Luckily for trick-or-treaters the decision was made to forge ahead with a total of 22 businesses, some only available for an hour or two, signing up to hand out candy and other treats. For years Douillard has organized the Downtown Trick r Treat annual festivities with her mother, Joan. She personally likes the 2 p.m. start time which is quiet, providing the perfect opportunity for toddlers, kids with sensory or sensitivity issues and anyone who might get overwhelmed to trick-or-treat before things pick up. She remembers the first Downtown Trick r Treat with about 15 locations signed up and running to Safeway to buy whatever she could to drop off after they ran out of candy in just 15 minutes. The biggest year for handing out candy at the Realm of Toys was before COVID with 744 kids. “After COVID we definitely saw a huge drop in numbers and it’s only slowly been increasing,” Douillard said, adding last year they hit over 500. This year they’re making sure they have enough for 650, and have spent between $600 to $800 to ensure costumed kids receive a mix of candy and even a comic or child’s book and possibly small seasonal toys, averaging about $1.25 per trick-or-treater. Helen Sandy has been taking photographs since she was 15 of her life in and around the Williams Lake First Nation. A fading Secwépemc tradition has been preserved thanks to the power of photography. On Thursday, Oct. 29, the Ckultenellcw Cultural Centre hosted the opening of *Preserving Salmon For Winter Food*, a photo exhibit created by Williams Lake First Nation Elder Helen Sandy. The series of striking photographs chronicles Indigenous fishing camps in Farwell Canyon over the course of 20 years, from salmon being caught using dip nets to being preserved via smoking. “For me, it’s passing on the knowledge. My two daughters know how (to prepare salmon), my grandchildren know how,” Sandy said. “In our community (salmon) is a delicacy; not too many people have it. It’s a dying tradition, not many people do it anymore.” Sandy’s journey with photography began when she was 15 and received an Instamatic camera that she used to take pictures of her friends and family. 1deca6730a0ff1a190da8242fcbdabcc.text: The City of Victoria has issued a safety warning after an owl attacked the same person twice in three days. On Oct. 4, bylaw staff received a complaint about a barred owl attacking a resident on the shared pedestrian and bike walkway along Dallas Road, between Douglas Road and the Beacon Hill Park Road exit. Signage was subsequently installed to raise awareness for park users regarding an “aggressive” barred owl in the area. “This activity is common and is typically a result of territory enforcement as adult owls look to establish new or protect existing territories,” the city said in a statement. This is the first time signage in Victoria has been installed to increase awareness for park users about owl attacks. Parks staff continue to monitor the situation and will remove the signage once the activity subsides. Ann Nightingale, a Rocky Point Bird Observatory volunteer, told Black Press in 2025 that territorial behaviour stems from the birds’ instinct to protect their young. Other times, however, owls attack people in the hopes of snagging a quick meal. “Sometimes … they mistake the movement of a ponytail or pompom as a prey item,” she said. “They primarily hunt by sound, so the swishing of hair on a jacket can sound like a small animal moving.” Nightingale recommended avoiding areas where attacks have recently occurred. “The owls that do this tend to be repeat offenders,” she said. “Once you know where they are, just give them a bit of space. They are usually defending a specific territory. If you need to walk that path, an open umbrella should keep the bird away or at least provide a barrier.” People with small cats and dogs are also advised to be cautious as owls can see them as prey. (Image Credit: Andy Devlin/Edmonton Oil Kings) EDMONTON — There were no Halloween scaries for Vit Zahejsky and the Kamloops Blazers at Rogers Place in Edmonton, as they skated to a 4-1 victory over the Edmonton Oil Kings on Saturday (Oct. 31) afternoon. The win also moved Blazers head coach Shaun Clouston into sole possession of fourth place on the Western Hockey League’s all-time wins leaderboard. Clouston picked up win number 627 to move past longtime WHL head coach Lorne Molleken. Zahejsky’s seventh goal of the season came via a shorthanded penalty shot at 13:51 of the first period as the Blazers took a 1-0 lead. Ty Bonkowski doubled the lead early in the second, but Edmonton pulled one back at 11:58 through Kayden Stroeder. He scored on a five-minute powerplay after Blazers defenceman Madden Tymchak was assessed a boarding major and game misconduct, but the Oil Kings weren’t able to beat Kaeden Tate a second time. Tate turned aside 20 of 21 shots to improve to 6-1 this season, with a 1.96 goals against average and a .937 save percentage. Logan Lanti scored his first of the season to make it 3-1 Kamloops early in the third period before Mikhail Cherepanov’s empty netter at 18:45 sealed the win for the visitors. Oil Kings netminder Parker Snell stopped 27 of 30 shots in a losing effort, as Edmonton dropped to 6-5-1-0 on the season. The Blazers moved to 8-4-2-0, to sit second in the B.C. Division and third in the Western Conference The Blazers head to Calgary next to face the 8-6-0-0 Hitmen in a Sunday (Nov. 1) matinee at Scotiabank Saddledome. Puck drop is set for 2:00 p.m. Alberta time. They’ll also play the Red Deer Rebels on Tuesday (Nov. 3) before returning home to host the Seattle Thunderbirds at Sandman Centre on Friday (Nov. 6).
